translation:
Zadeshwar

In Zadeshwar lived the descendants of Gyaniji; they may still be there today. At Mangleshwar, Jivanji had delivered the wife of Keshavdas, Rambai, from the spirit of Bhoja Gujar that had entered her body — this Keshavdas was from this very Zadeshwar, and so Keshavdas is known by the name Keshavdas Zadeshwariya. This Keshavdas was a goldsmith (soni) by caste.

Devotee Narsinhbhai Ramji, of the Naria neighbourhood (khadki) of Vadodara, was employed at Vadsal. While he was there singing the aarti (devotional hymn), a goldsmith living nearby, overhearing him, began to say: "This is our aarti, to Padmanabh." Narsinhbhai replied: "No, this is our aarti." As this pulling back and forth continued between them, the goldsmith said: "We are Uda Sonis (goldsmiths of the Uda order)." Saying this, he gave him a handwritten manuscript. Narsinhbhai had shown this manuscript to me, but today it is no longer with his heir Vitthalbhai — which is a matter of regret.

This episode thus recalls an event from the lifetime of Jivanji. So this Zadeshwar too is a holy place.

Note: Keshavdas Soni may have become an Uda [renunciate], but the heirs of Krishnadas of Sardarpur did not give up their brahmin status and remained brahmins, and so the mahants of Sardarpur are brahmins. In the same way, it seems the heirs of Keshavdas did not give up their status as goldsmiths, and so remained goldsmiths. But it has come to be known that the last among them was, in this way, a goldsmith known as Uda Soni.
